25.text: The Qur'an's invitation to more than the minimum is an invitation to knowing God like a fasting person knows hunger: intimately and undoubtedly. This chapter defines the difference between knowing God and knowing about God, and then explores how He comes to be known.

27.text: The comparison with hunger is an example of this knowledge's attainment and not its extent. As the Sheikh puts it frankly, "the more you know, the more bewildered you will become".

30.text: Imam Khomeini caveats the prominent position of learning with a warning, writing that "a learning that does not bring faith with it is the greatest of veils". Yet the veil cannot be avoided, only passed through: "one has to approach a veil in order to tear it into shreds".

31.before_override: They are brought near to God and know Him by presence: a veil is removed, rather than a definition learned. Their knowing is present to the soul, as hunger is present to the one who fasts.
31.text: Their nearness to God comes as the veils of the heart are unravelled: an action and a process that cannot be substituted by learning a definition. The knowing of the ʿurafaʾ is as present to their souls as hunger is to the one who fasts.

35.text: A person during the meal of iftar cannot understand hunger as sharply as they will understand it during the next day's fast, despite having spent most of their day hungry. There is no substitute for arriving in that moment. In this way, mystics seek to arrive at God.
